case_title: Sri Bhagwan v. State of U.P.
accused_occupation: Small grocery shop owner (as argued on behalf of the appellant; not a court finding)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (conviction); IPC s.326 (originally registered offence)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PWs 1 and 3); dying declaration (s.161 CrPC statement treated as s.32(1) declaration); medical evidence (injury report and post-mortem); recovery of gloves with chemical report
aggravating_circumstances: Acid attack causing extensive burns and death of the victim; accused reportedly attempted to flee on being seen
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; sentenced to life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: On the night of 26 May 1980, at about 10.45 p.m., two local residents who were guarding their colony nearby heard screams from a bus stand about 250 yards away and ran to the spot. They said they saw the accused pouring acid on the victim, who was suffering burn injuries. They said the accused was heard saying he would pay a sum of money that day. When the witnesses approached, the accused tried to run away but was caught by bystanders. The accused and the victim were taken to a police station by about 11.10 p.m., and a complaint by one of the witnesses led to an FIR under s.326 IPC. An officer recorded the victim's statement within about ten minutes so that he could be sent to hospital. In that statement the victim said the accused had thrown acid on him. A doctor examined the victim and recorded superficial burns on the face, neck, tongue, back, and other parts of the body. The victim died the next day from the burns, and a post-mortem was conducted. The investigating officer inspected the scene and collected an acid bottle, a bag, and gloves. A chemical report found acid on burnt rubber gloves. No acid marks were found on the accused's body. The defence pointed to the absence of a street light on the site plan, the victim's tongue injury, and the failure to seize the victim's clothes for chemical examination.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from extensive acid burns (superficial burns on face, neck, tongue, back and other body parts)
premeditation_planning: Not expressly found as premeditation; court noted the accused took precautions (wearing gloves) while throwing acid
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of PWs 1 and 3; victim's s.161 CrPC statement (Ex Ka-2) accepted as dying declaration; injury report Ka-17 and post-mortem report Ka-13 with PW-5 testimony; chemical report Ka-18 on burnt rubber gloves
witness_credibility: PWs 1 and 3 found convincing, natural and credible; not interested witnesses; not stock witnesses; no prior deposition in other cases shown; their statements were not diluted by their account of the victim's statement
post_offence_conduct: Attempted to flee the scene and was caught by bystanders; no other post-offence conduct noted
trial_duration: offence: 26.05.1980; trial judgment: 06.09.1982; High Court: 28.11.2008; Supreme Court: 06 December 2012
legal_representation: Accused: M.P. Shorawala, Jyoti Saxena, Ranbir Yadav, Anzu K. Varkey and Shashi Kiran. State: Ratnakar Dash, Alka Sinha and Anuvrat Sharma
investigation_status: FIR registered under s.326 IPC; case altered to s.302 IPC after death; site inspected and articles collected; charge-sheet filed; chemical examination completed; investigation taken over by S.H.O. on 28.05.1980; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Defence argued non-compliance with Police Regulation 115 (two witnesses, signatures for dying declaration); court held it did not apply to a s.161 statement. Clothes of the deceased not sent for chemical examination; court held this isolated and not fatal
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Eyewitnesses were strangers with no reason to implicate the accused; statement of the victim was a valid dying declaration under s.32(1) Evidence Act; FIR and bringing both persons to the police station showed the case was truly projected; the Police Regulation 115 point was not raised below and was irrelevant
defence_argument: Witnesses could not have seen the incident; victim with tongue burns could not make a statement; s.161 statement was not a valid dying declaration (no Police Regulation 115 attestation); no acid marks on accused; witnesses were stock witnesses; arrest suppressed; absence of street light on site plan; accused was grieving his father
legal_principle_applied: A s.161 CrPC statement by a victim who later dies may be treated as a dying declaration under s.32(1) Evidence Act and carry the same credence; conviction may rest on a true and voluntary dying declaration without corroboration; eyewitnesses assessed for interest and stock-witness status; police regulation does not override statutory provisions
precedent_relied_upon: Ravikumar alias Kutti Ravi v. State of T.N. 2006 (9) SCC 240 (relied on); Babudas v. State of M.P. 2003 (9) SCC 86 (held inapplicable); Baldev Singh v. State of Punjab 2009 (6) SCC 564 (held inapplicable); Jai Prakash and Others v. State of Haryana 1998 (7) SCC 284 (cited); Suresh Chaudhary v. State of Bihar 2003 (4) SCC 128 (held inapplicable)
